name: Speckled lentiginous naevus syndrome
aliases: partial unilateral lentiginosis with neurological features

reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Neurocutaneous Disorders (current reference texts)
clinicalPearls: Characterised by a speckled lentiginous naevus (naevus spilus) with a background café-au-lait patch studded with darker macules or papules, together with extracutaneous anomalies
It is considered a mosaic condition, with post-zygotic activating HRAS or KRAS variants reported in affected lesions
The syndromic form is associated with segmental neurological disturbance, including dysaesthesia, hyperhidrosis and muscular weakness in the affected segment
When it occurs alongside an organoid naevus sebaceus it forms part of phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica
Melanocytic naevi within the lesion carry a small risk of melanoma, so surveillance of changing lesions is important
Neurological and skeletal anomalies may accompany extensive disease, warranting broader assessment
Management is generic: dermatological surveillance of the naevus, neurological evaluation of segmental symptoms and multidisciplinary support
reference.pathophysiology: Speckled lentiginous naevus syndrome is a mosaic disorder arising from a post-zygotic activating variant in the RAS pathway, with HRAS and KRAS implicated, affecting a clone of neural-crest-derived melanocytes during development. This produces the background tan café-au-lait patch with superimposed darker melanocytic macules and papules characteristic of a naevus spilus, distributed segmentally. When the same or a partner clone involves peripheral nerve, muscle or skeletal tissue, the syndrome's segmental sensory disturbance, hyperhidrosis, weakness and skeletal anomalies develop. The melanocytic component carries a small potential for malignant transformation, accounting for the recognised, though low, melanoma risk within these lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated naevus spilus without systemic features
additionalInvestigations: Skin examination and dermoscopy of the naevus and its speckles
Skin biopsy of any atypical or changing focus within the lesion
Neurological assessment of segmental sensory, sudomotor and motor function
MRI where central or peripheral neurological involvement is suspected
Skeletal imaging where asymmetry or deformity is present
Molecular testing of lesional tissue for HRAS/KRAS variants where available
redFlags: Change in colour, size or surface of a melanocytic focus suggesting melanoma
Progressive segmental weakness or sensory loss
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally good for limited disease; the main long-term concern is the small melanoma risk within the melanocytic component, while extensive neurological or skeletal involvement in the syndromic form determines additional morbidity.
pitfalls: Assuming a naevus spilus is always isolated and not evaluating for segmental neurological features
Confusing the background patch with a café-au-lait macule of neurofibromatosis
Failing to biopsy a changing melanocytic focus within the lesion
Overlooking its overlap with phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica when an organoid naevus is also present
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
management: Regular dermatological surveillance with dermoscopy for melanoma arising within the melanocytic component
Biopsy or excision of any atypical, changing or suspicious focus within the naevus
Neurological assessment and symptomatic management of segmental dysaesthesia, hyperhidrosis and muscular weakness
MRI and specialist referral where central or peripheral neurological involvement is suspected
Skeletal imaging and orthopaedic input for associated asymmetry or deformity
Coordinate multidisciplinary care between dermatology, neurology and relevant specialists in extensive disease
Counsel that this is a mosaic post-zygotic (HRAS/KRAS) condition, generally not inherited, with molecular testing of lesional tissue where available
